energy-materials-001.question: When a lithium-ion battery (graphite anode, LiCoO₂ cathode) discharges, which correctly describes the movement of lithium ions and electrons?
choices: Li⁺ moves through the electrolyte from the negative electrode to the positive electrode, and electrons flow through the external circuit from the negative electrode to the positive electrode
Li⁺ moves through the electrolyte from the negative electrode to the positive electrode, and electrons flow through the external circuit from the positive electrode to the negative electrode
Li⁺ moves through the electrolyte from the positive electrode to the negative electrode, and electrons flow through the external circuit from the negative electrode to the positive electrode
energy-materials-001.explanation: On discharge, lithium stored between the graphite layers splits into Li⁺ and an electron and leaves the negative electrode. Li⁺ moves through the electrolyte (and separator) to the positive electrode and enters between the layers of LiCoO₂, while the electrons flow through the external circuit to the positive electrode as well, doing work on the way. Electrons flow from the negative to the positive electrode, so the current flows from positive to negative; the choice with electrons flowing from positive to negative confuses the direction of current with the flow of electrons. The choice with Li⁺ moving from positive to negative gives the direction of Li⁺ during charging: on charge, an external power supply pushes electrons into the negative electrode and Li⁺ also returns from the positive to the negative electrode. On both discharge and charge, Li⁺ and electrons move in the same direction, keeping the charge on both electrodes balanced. Because Li⁺ simply shuttles between the electrodes while the electrode frameworks are preserved, it is also called a rocking-chair battery.

energy-materials-002.question: Which correctly pairs lithium-ion battery cathode materials with their crystal structures?
choices: LiCoO₂ is spinel, LiMn₂O₄ is olivine and LiFePO₄ is layered rock salt
LiCoO₂ is layered rock salt, LiMn₂O₄ is spinel and LiFePO₄ is olivine
LiCoO₂ is olivine, LiMn₂O₄ is layered rock salt and LiFePO₄ is spinel
energy-materials-002.explanation: LiCoO₂ has the layered rock salt structure (α-NaFeO₂ type), with Li layers and Co layers alternating within close-packed oxygen, and Li⁺ moves two-dimensionally between the layers. LiMn₂O₄ is a spinel, with three-dimensionally connected Li⁺ pathways within its Mn–O framework and an operating voltage of about 4 V. LiFePO₄ has the olivine structure, the same as the mineral olivine, in which Li⁺ moves along one-dimensional tunnels in a framework of PO₄ tetrahedra and FeO₆ octahedra, with an operating voltage of about 3.4 V. The other two choices shuffle the names of these three structures. Layered, spinel and olivine are the three basic structures used to classify cathode materials.

energy-materials-003.question: When a graphite anode is fully lithiated, it becomes LiC₆. Which value is closest to the theoretical capacity of graphite (per mass of graphite)? Take the atomic mass of carbon as 12.01, the Faraday constant as 96485 C/mol and 1 mAh = 3.6 C.
choices: About 2230 mAh/g
About 339 mAh/g
About 372 mAh/g
energy-materials-003.explanation: One mole of C₆ (72.06 g) takes up one mole of Li⁺ and one mole of electrons, so the stored charge is 96485 C. The capacity per mass is Q = nF/(3.6M) = 1 × 96485 / (3.6 × 72.06) ≈ 372 mAh/g. About 339 mAh/g uses the mass of LiC₆ including Li (78.99 g/mol) in the denominator; anode capacity is normally expressed per mass of lithium-free graphite. About 2230 mAh/g is the mistake of assuming one lithium per carbon atom. Real graphite anodes are used at about 350–360 mAh/g, close to the theoretical value, and materials such as silicon are being researched to achieve higher capacity.

energy-materials-004.question: For the olivine cathode material LiFePO₄, assuming all the lithium is extracted and reinserted via the Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ reaction, which value is closest to the theoretical capacity? Take the formula weight of LiFePO₄ as 157.8 g/mol, the Faraday constant as 96485 C/mol and 1 mAh = 3.6 C.
choices: About 170 mAh/g
About 85 mAh/g
About 340 mAh/g
energy-materials-004.explanation: One mole of Li⁺ leaves one mole of LiFePO₄ and Fe²⁺ is oxidized to Fe³⁺, so one mole of electrons is transferred. The theoretical capacity is Q = nF/(3.6M) = 1 × 96485 / (3.6 × 157.8) ≈ 170 mAh/g. About 340 mAh/g counts two electrons in the reaction, but the change from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ involves one electron. About 85 mAh/g divides by 2 somewhere along the way. LiFePO₄ can in practice deliver around 160 mAh/g, close to the theoretical value, but its average voltage of about 3.4 V is relatively low, so its energy per mass is smaller than that of layered oxide cathodes.

energy-materials-005.question: Which is a characteristic of the olivine LiFePO₄ cathode?
choices: Li⁺ moves two-dimensionally between layers, and extracting more than half the Li on charge destabilizes the layered structure
It has a spinel structure with three-dimensional Li⁺ pathways, and capacity loss from Mn dissolution is a challenge
Strong P–O bonds make it reluctant to release oxygen, but its electronic conductivity is low, so it is used as fine carbon-coated particles
energy-materials-005.explanation: In LiFePO₄, oxygen is bound to P by strong covalent bonds in PO₄ tetrahedra, so it rarely releases oxygen even on overcharge or at high temperatures, giving it excellent thermal safety. On the other hand, Li⁺ diffusion is confined to one-dimensional tunnels and the electronic conductivity is extremely low, so the particles are made as small as about 100 nm and their surfaces are coated with carbon. Two-dimensional movement of Li⁺ between layers and structural instability when more than about half the Li is extracted are characteristics of layered rock salt LiCoO₂. Three-dimensional pathways with Mn dissolution as a challenge describe spinel LiMn₂O₄.

energy-materials-006.question: Which statement about silicon (Si) as an anode material is correct?
choices: Its theoretical capacity is smaller than that of graphite, but its volume changes by less than 1% on cycling, so it has a long life
Its theoretical capacity is about ten times that of graphite, but it swells more than threefold on lithiation and degrades easily
Its theoretical capacity is about the same as graphite, but its metal-like electronic conductivity suits fast charging
energy-materials-006.explanation: Si alloys with lithium, and when it reacts as far as Li₁₅Si₄ at room temperature its theoretical capacity is about 3600 mAh/g per mass of Si, about ten times that of graphite (372 mAh/g). However, its volume swells about three- to fourfold on lithiation, so with repeated cycling the particles crack and become electrically isolated, the electrolyte decomposes on the newly exposed surfaces to re-form the SEI (solid electrolyte interphase), and lithium is gradually lost. In practice, therefore, small amounts of Si or SiO are blended into graphite, or Si is made into nanoparticles, to limit the effect of expansion. Hardly any volume change is a characteristic of lithium titanate (Li₄Ti₅O₁₂); even graphite changes by only about 10%. Si has low electronic conductivity, so the statement that it suits fast charging is also wrong.

energy-materials-007.question: Which statement about sulfide solid electrolytes used in all-solid-state batteries is correct?
choices: Some match organic liquid electrolytes in ionic conductivity and densify by pressing alone, but they react with moisture to release hydrogen sulfide

Their ionic conductivity is at least three orders of magnitude lower than organic liquid electrolytes, but they are so stable that they do not react even with moisture in air, so no dry environment is needed
They are hard and hardly deform, so their particles neither bond nor conduct Li⁺ unless they are sintered together at high temperatures well above 1000 °C
energy-materials-007.explanation: Some sulfide solid electrolytes, such as Li₁₀GeP₂S₁₂ (LGPS), Li₇P₃S₁₁ and argyrodite-type Li₆PS₅Cl, show room-temperature ionic conductivities of 10⁻³–10⁻² S/cm, comparable to organic liquid electrolytes (about 10⁻² S/cm). Sulfides are soft and deform easily, so another advantage is that simply pressing the powder at room temperature gives good contact between particles and with the electrodes. On the other hand, they tend to react with moisture in the air and release toxic hydrogen sulfide, so they must be handled in a dry environment. Requiring high-temperature sintering to densify is characteristic of oxide electrolytes such as garnet-type Li₇La₃Zr₂O₁₂ (LLZO). LLZO is relatively stable in air and reacts little with lithium metal, but being hard, it is difficult to form interfaces with the electrodes.

energy-materials-008.question: Which statement about the electrolyte of a polymer electrolyte fuel cell (PEFC, also called a PEM fuel cell) is correct?
choices: It is a ceramic membrane that conducts oxide ions (O²⁻), so it is operated above 700 °C to raise its conductivity
It is a molten carbonate in which carbonate ions move to the fuel electrode, so it is operated at about 650 °C
It is a fluorinated polymer membrane with sulfonic acid groups that conducts protons when wet, so it runs at about 100 °C or below
energy-materials-008.explanation: The electrolyte of a PEFC is a polymer membrane with a fluoropolymer backbone and side chains bearing sulfonic acid groups (−SO₃H). When the membrane absorbs water, hydrophilic channels lined with sulfonic acid groups form, and protons move through them together with water. Conductivity drops sharply when the membrane dries, so humidification is needed, and to avoid losing water from the membrane the operating temperature is kept at about 100 °C or below, typically about 80 °C. Using a ceramic membrane that conducts O²⁻ above 700 °C describes the solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC), which uses stabilized zirconia and similar materials. A molten carbonate electrolyte operated at about 650 °C is used in the molten carbonate fuel cell (MCFC). The differences in electrolyte determine each type's operating temperature, usable fuels and catalysts.

energy-materials-009.question: The standard Gibbs energy change of the reaction forming liquid water from hydrogen and oxygen, H₂ + 1/2 O₂ → H₂O(l), is −237 kJ/mol at 25 °C. Which value is closest to the theoretical emf of a fuel cell using this reaction? Take the Faraday constant as 96485 C/mol.
choices: About 2.46 V
About 1.23 V
About 0.61 V
energy-materials-009.explanation: The theoretical emf is E = −ΔG/(nF), and when 1 mol of H₂ reacts, 2 mol of electrons are transferred, so n = 2. E = 237×10³ / (2 × 96485) ≈ 1.23 V. About 2.46 V takes n = 1, and about 0.61 V combines the number of electrons per mole of O₂, n = 4, with ΔG per mole of H₂. The ratio of the Gibbs energy change to the enthalpy change of the reaction (−286 kJ/mol), 237/286 ≈ 83%, is a guide to the theoretical efficiency at 25 °C. In real cells, electrode overpotentials and electrolyte resistance lower the operating voltage to about 0.6–0.8 V.

energy-materials-010.question: For a single-junction solar cell, there is an optimum band gap of the absorber semiconductor that maximizes the theoretical efficiency (about 1.1–1.4 eV under terrestrial sunlight). Which is the correct reason?
choices: A small band gap gives a low voltage and loses excess energy as heat, while a large one leaves more photons unabsorbed
The larger the band gap, the more photons are absorbed, but mobility falls, so the current decreases
The smaller the band gap, the less recombination, but because sunlight has the same intensity at all wavelengths, the gain levels off somewhere
energy-materials-010.explanation: A photon is absorbed only when its energy is at least the band gap Eg, and the energy in excess of Eg is handed to the lattice as heat by the carriers (thermalization loss). In addition, the open-circuit voltage cannot exceed Eg/q. With a small Eg more photons are absorbed but less energy can be extracted per photon; with a large Eg the voltage is higher, but photons with energy below Eg are not absorbed and pass through. Balancing these, the Shockley–Queisser theoretical efficiency under standard terrestrial sunlight (AM1.5) is high, about 32–33%, over the range of about 1.1–1.4 eV, with a maximum of about 33% at about 1.34 eV. The statement that a larger Eg increases absorption is backward. The intensity of sunlight varies greatly with wavelength and is not constant.

energy-materials-011.question: A thermoelectric material at 300 K has a Seebeck coefficient of 200 µV/K, an electrical conductivity of 1.0×10⁵ S/m and a thermal conductivity of 1.5 W/(m·K). Which value is closest to the dimensionless figure of merit ZT = S²σT/κ?
choices: About 0.0027
About 0.8
About 4000
energy-materials-011.explanation: The power factor is S²σ = (200×10⁻⁶)² × 1.0×10⁵ = 4.0×10⁻⁸ × 1.0×10⁵ = 4.0×10⁻³ W/(m·K²). Multiplying by the temperature and dividing by the thermal conductivity gives ZT = 4.0×10⁻³ × 300 / 1.5 = 0.8. About 0.0027 forgets to multiply by the temperature T; ZT becomes dimensionless only once temperature is included. About 4000 forgets to square the Seebeck coefficient. Bi₂Te₃-based materials used near room temperature have a ZT of about 1, and the larger ZT, the closer the heat-to-electricity conversion efficiency approaches the Carnot efficiency set by the hot- and cold-side temperatures.

energy-materials-012.question: Which is a correct strategy for increasing the thermoelectric figure of merit ZT?
choices: Raising the carrier concentration to metallic levels increases both the Seebeck coefficient and the electrical conductivity at the same time, so ZT rises sharply
Lowering the electrical conductivity and raising the thermal conductivity lets heat pass through the element faster, so a temperature difference is easier to maintain and ZT rises
Scatter phonons with nanostructures or heavy atoms to lower the lattice thermal conductivity while disturbing electrical conduction as little as possible
energy-materials-012.explanation: To make ZT = S²σT/κ large, the Seebeck coefficient S and electrical conductivity σ must be high and the thermal conductivity κ low. However, raising the carrier concentration increases σ but decreases S, and also increases the heat carried by electrons (the Wiedemann–Franz law), so the optimum is a nearly degenerate semiconductor with a carrier concentration of about 10¹⁹–10²⁰ cm⁻³. At metallic levels S becomes too small. A promising strategy is therefore to scatter only the phonons, which carry most of the heat, using nanostructured interfaces or the rattling of heavy atoms, to lower the lattice thermal conductivity; this is described as “phonon glass, electron crystal.” Lowering σ and raising κ moves ZT down.

energy-materials-013.question: In a lithium-ion battery with a graphite negative electrode, an SEI (solid electrolyte interphase) film forms on the electrode surface during the first charge. Which statement about this film is correct?
choices: It is metal dissolved from the positive electrode and deposited on the negative one; it conducts electrons well, lowering the internal resistance and raising the capacity
It forms from reductive decomposition of the electrolyte; it passes Li⁺ but hardly conducts electrons, suppressing further decomposition at the cost of an irreversible capacity
It dissolves at every discharge and re-forms at every charge; it consumes no Li, so it has no effect at all on the battery capacity
energy-materials-013.explanation: The graphite negative electrode operates at a low potential of about 0.1 V versus Li, below the range in which organic electrolytes are stable. During the first charge, the solvent and salt of the electrolyte are therefore reductively decomposed on the electrode surface, and the products form a thin film called the SEI. The SEI passes Li⁺ but hardly conducts electrons, so once it has formed it suppresses further decomposition of the electrolyte and lets the cell charge and discharge stably. Li is consumed in forming the film, however, so part of the first charge capacity becomes an irreversible capacity that is not recovered on discharge. Deposition of metal dissolved from the positive electrode is a degradation mechanism distinct from the SEI. The SEI is not rebuilt at every cycle, and the statement that it consumes no Li is also wrong.

energy-materials-014.question: In CdTe and CIGS (Cu(In,Ga)Se₂) thin-film solar cells an absorber a few µm thick is enough, whereas crystalline silicon cells use a thickness of 100 µm or more. What is the main reason?
choices: The band gap of silicon is larger than the energy of visible light, so it cannot absorb any light unless it is thick
CdTe and CIGS have electron mobilities orders of magnitude higher than silicon, so all generated carriers are collected even in a thin layer
CdTe and CIGS are direct-gap materials with large absorption coefficients, whereas silicon is indirect-gap with small absorption near the band edge
energy-materials-014.explanation: In a direct-gap semiconductor, the absorption coefficient for light above the band gap is large, 10⁴–10⁵ cm⁻¹, so a CdTe or CIGS layer a few µm thick absorbs most of the sunlight. Silicon is an indirect-gap semiconductor, in which absorption requires the participation of a phonon, so its absorption coefficient for near-infrared light close to the band gap is small, and absorbing that light fully takes a thickness of tens to hundreds of µm. Surface texturing, which sends light obliquely to lengthen its path, is also used. The band gap of silicon is about 1.12 eV, smaller than the energy of visible light (about 1.6–3.1 eV), so silicon does absorb visible light. Nor are the mobilities of CdTe or CIGS orders of magnitude higher than that of silicon.

energy-materials-015.question: At 25°C, the reaction H₂ + 1/2 O₂ → H₂O(l) has a standard Gibbs energy change of −237 kJ/mol and a standard enthalpy change of −286 kJ/mol. Which is closest to the theoretical efficiency of a fuel cell using this reaction (the maximum fraction of the reaction's enthalpy change that can be taken out as electricity)?
choices: About 83%
About 17%
About 100%
energy-materials-015.explanation: The maximum energy a fuel cell can deliver as electricity is the magnitude of the Gibbs energy change, so the theoretical efficiency is ΔG/ΔH = 237/286 ≈ 0.83, or about 83%. The remaining TΔS, about 17% (49 kJ/mol), is released as heat even when the reaction runs reversibly; 17% mistakes the fraction of this heat for the efficiency. A fuel cell is not a heat engine and is not bound by the Carnot efficiency, but for a reaction in which entropy decreases the TΔS portion must be rejected as heat, so the efficiency cannot be 100%. In real cells, losses from overpotentials and resistance lower the operating voltage below the theoretical EMF of about 1.23 V, and the efficiency falls further.

energy-materials-016.question: Under standard illumination (100 mW/cm²), a solar cell has an open-circuit voltage of 0.70 V, a short-circuit current density of 40 mA/cm² and a fill factor of 0.80. Which is closest to its conversion efficiency?
choices: About 22%
About 28%
About 18%
energy-materials-016.explanation: The maximum power is the product of the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current density times the fill factor: Pmax = 0.70 × 40 × 0.80 = 22.4 mW/cm². Dividing by the incident 100 mW/cm² gives an efficiency of about 22%. About 28% forgets the fill factor. On the current–voltage curve, the voltage is zero at short circuit, where the current is largest, and the current is zero at open circuit, where the voltage is largest, so no power is delivered at either point, and the actual maximum power point is smaller than Voc × Jsc. That ratio is the fill factor. About 18% applies the fill factor twice. The fill factor falls when the series resistance is large or the shunt leakage current is high.

energy-materials-017.question: Sodium-ion batteries mainly use hard carbon (non-graphitizable carbon) for the negative electrode, rather than the graphite common in lithium-ion batteries. What is the reason?
choices: Na⁺ is smaller than Li⁺ and escapes easily from between the graphite layers, so it cannot be held after charging and self-discharge is large
Na hardly forms a stable compound between graphite layers, so capacity is tiny; hard carbon stores Na in disordered layers and pores instead
Too much Na enters between the graphite layers, the volume swells by more than three times, and the graphite particles crack on repeated cycling
energy-materials-017.explanation: Lithium enters graphite up to LiC₆, but sodium forms almost no stable intercalation compound, and in ordinary electrolytes the capacity is tiny. The larger potassium forms KC₈, so the cause is considered to be the thermodynamic instability of Na–graphite compounds rather than simply the size of the ion. Hard carbon consists of small graphite-like layers stacked in a disordered way, with wide interlayer gaps and fine pores, and storing Na there gives a practical capacity. The ionic radius of Na⁺, about 0.102 nm, is larger than that of Li⁺ (about 0.076 nm), so calling it smaller is the wrong way round. Swelling to more than three times the volume is a problem of silicon negative electrodes, which alloy with Li.

energy-materials-018.question: In a layered lithium-ion positive electrode Li(Ni,Mn,Co)O₂, which statement correctly describes the trade-off of raising the Ni fraction (making it Ni-rich)?
choices: The capacity decreases, but Ni binds oxygen strongly, so oxygen is less likely to be released even on deep charge and safety improves
The crystal structure changes to the olivine type and the Li⁺ pathways become one-dimensional, so power decreases but life becomes longer
The capacity increases, but Ni²⁺ of similar size tends to enter the Li⁺ layers, and the thermal stability in the deeply charged state also decreases
energy-materials-018.explanation: In layered Li(Ni,Mn,Co)O₂ the capacity is carried mainly by the Ni²⁺/Ni³⁺/Ni⁴⁺ redox, so more Ni gives more capacity at the same charging voltage. However, the ionic radius of Ni²⁺ (about 0.069 nm) is close to that of Li⁺ (about 0.076 nm), so cation mixing, in which Ni enters the Li layers, occurs easily, blocking Li⁺ pathways and lowering capacity and power. In addition, when much Li has been removed the amount of unstable Ni⁴⁺ increases, and oxygen is released more readily at high temperature. Mn stabilizes the structure and Co suppresses cation mixing. Saying that oxygen release becomes harder is the wrong way round, and the structure remains layered when the composition changes, so it does not become olivine.

energy-materials-019.question: Activated carbon with a specific surface area of 1500 m²/g is used for an electrode of an electric double-layer capacitor. If the double-layer capacitance at the surface in contact with the electrolyte is 10 µF/cm² and the entire surface is used, which is closest to the capacitance per gram of electrode?
choices: About 1.5 F/g
About 150 F/g
About 0.015 F/g
energy-materials-019.explanation: 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², so the specific surface area is 1500 × 10⁴ = 1.5×10⁷ cm²/g. The capacitance is 10×10⁻⁶ F/cm² × 1.5×10⁷ cm²/g = 150 F/g. About 1.5 F/g converts 1 m² wrongly as 100 cm², and about 0.015 F/g multiplies without converting between m² and cm². An electric double-layer capacitor stores charge simply by ions lining up at the electrode surface, with no chemical reaction, so it can be charged and discharged rapidly and has a long cycle life. Its energy, however, is E = CV²/2 and is limited by the voltage range in which the electrolyte does not decompose, so its energy density is smaller than that of a battery.

energy-materials-020.question: Lithium metal has a theoretical capacity of about 3860 mAh/g as a negative electrode, more than ten times that of graphite, but it is difficult to use in rechargeable batteries. What is the main reason?
choices: On charging Li grows in branched forms that can pierce the separator and short the cell, and SEI keeps forming on fresh surfaces, consuming Li and electrolyte
The electrode potential of lithium metal is close to that of the positive electrode, so the cell voltage is below 1 V and almost no energy can be extracted
On charging Li enters between layers as in graphite, so the capacity is limited to 372 mAh/g like graphite and the large theoretical capacity cannot be used
energy-materials-020.explanation: The theoretical capacity of Li is F/(3.6 × 6.94) ≈ 3860 mAh/g. On charging, however, Li simply deposits on the electrode surface, so it tends to grow as dendrites or mossy deposits from places where the current concentrates; if these pierce the separator, they cause an internal short and heating. Each deposition exposes fresh Li to the electrolyte and forms new SEI, consuming Li and electrolyte and lowering the coulombic efficiency and life. Lithium metal has one of the lowest standard electrode potentials, about −3.04 V, and gives a high voltage when combined with a positive electrode, so the low-voltage explanation is the wrong way round. Metallic Li deposits without forming an intercalation compound, so it is not limited to the capacity of graphite.

energy-materials-021.question: A thermoelectric material with an average figure of merit ZT = 1.0 generates power between a hot side at Th = 500 K and a cold side at Tc = 300 K. Which value is closest to the maximum conversion efficiency η = [(Th − Tc)/Th] × (√(1 + ZT) − 1)/(√(1 + ZT) + Tc/Th)?
choices: About 8.2%
About 21%
About 40%
energy-materials-021.explanation: The Carnot efficiency is (500 − 300)/500 = 0.40. With √(1 + 1.0) ≈ 1.414, the material factor is (1.414 − 1)/(1.414 + 0.60) ≈ 0.206, so η = 0.40 × 0.206 ≈ 0.082, about 8.2%. About 40% is the Carnot efficiency itself, the limit as ZT goes to infinity. About 21% gives only the material factor and forgets to multiply by the Carnot efficiency. Even with ZT = 1, only about a fifth of the Carnot efficiency is obtained, so thermoelectric generation suits uses that exploit its lack of moving parts and its ability to use small temperature differences in waste heat. Raising ZT to 2 gives about 13% under the same temperatures.

energy-materials-022.question: When a polymer electrolyte fuel cell (PEFC) runs on hydrogen made by reforming natural gas or similar fuels, the carbon monoxide (CO) it contains must be removed to a very low concentration. Which is the main reason?
choices: CO reacts with the sulfonic acid groups of the polymer membrane and turns them all into carbonates that no longer conduct protons
CO crosses to the cathode and burns with oxygen there, and the heat released dries out the membrane above 100°C
CO adsorbs strongly on the platinum catalyst, blocking hydrogen reaction sites, and hardly desorbs at the low operating temperature
energy-materials-022.explanation: At the PEFC anode, the reaction H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ takes place on the platinum catalyst surface. CO adsorbs on platinum more strongly than hydrogen and hardly desorbs at operating temperatures below 100°C, so even small amounts block the reaction sites and greatly reduce the voltage (poisoning). Reformed gas is therefore cleaned to low CO levels by steps such as selective oxidation of CO, and CO-tolerant platinum-ruthenium alloy catalysts are also used. In high-temperature solid oxide fuel cells, CO does not poison the catalyst and can even be used as fuel. The explanations that CO turns the membrane into carbonates or burns at the cathode and dries the membrane are mechanistically wrong.

energy-materials-023.question: In a tandem solar cell that stacks two cells with different band gaps, which combination of the layer placed on the light-incident side and the reason is correct?
choices: The smaller-gap layer goes on top so it absorbs all the light first, and the lower layer converts the heat released into electricity
The larger-gap layer goes on top, using high-energy photons at a high voltage, and the lower layer absorbs the light passing through
Two layers with the same gap are stacked, the lower one absorbing light the upper one missed, so the current is doubled
energy-materials-023.explanation: In a single-junction cell, the excess energy of photons above the band gap becomes heat, and photons below the gap are not absorbed. A tandem cell puts the larger-gap layer on the light-incident side to extract high-energy photons at a high voltage, and the lower, smaller-gap layer absorbs the lower-energy light that passes through. This reduces thermalization losses and lets the cell exceed the theoretical limit of a single junction. With the smaller-gap layer on top, nearly all the light would be absorbed there and never reach the larger-gap layer, and there is no mechanism for converting the heat into electricity. Stacking identical layers does not change the loss mechanisms, and in series connection the current does not double.

energy-materials-024.question: A spinel LiMn₂O₄ cathode is cheap and thermally stable, but its capacity tends to fade when it is cycled, especially at high temperature (for example 55°C). Which is the main cause?
choices: Mn⁴⁺ is reduced to manganese metal, which grows as dendrites from the cathode surface and pierces the separator
The Li⁺ pathways in spinel are one-dimensional, so at high temperature they become blocked and Li⁺ can no longer move
Mn²⁺ formed by disproportionation of Mn³⁺ dissolves into the electrolyte and deposits on the anode, damaging the SEI
energy-materials-024.explanation: LiMn₂O₄ contains Mn³⁺ and Mn⁴⁺ in equal amounts, and Mn³⁺ at the surface disproportionates as 2Mn³⁺ → Mn⁴⁺ + Mn²⁺. The Mn²⁺ dissolves into the electrolyte; acid formed by electrolyte decomposition speeds this up, and high temperature accelerates it further. The dissolved manganese deposits on the anode, damaging the SEI and consuming lithium, so capacity fades. When the electrode is deeply discharged and Mn³⁺ increases, the Jahn-Teller effect also distorts the crystal. Countermeasures include substituting other elements for part of the Mn and coating the surface. The pathways in spinel are three-dimensional; one-dimensional pathways belong to olivine. Manganese metal growing as dendrites is wrong; dendritic deposition is a problem of lithium metal at the anode.

energy-materials-025.question: The theoretical capacity of LiCoO₂ (with all Li extracted and reinserted) is about 274 mAh/g, but in ordinary use with a charge cutoff of about 4.2 V only about 140 mAh/g is obtained. Which is the main reason?
choices: Taking x in Li₁₋ₓCoO₂ beyond about 0.5 damages the structure by phase changes and oxygen release, so only about half the Li is used
Co³⁺ is never oxidized to Co⁴⁺, so only the Li in the outermost few layers of each particle can leave, and the Li left inside cannot move
Capacity is set only by the amount of Li⁺ dissolved in the electrolyte and has nothing to do with the Li in the cathode crystal
energy-materials-025.explanation: Removing x of Li oxidizes Co³⁺ to Co⁴⁺, giving Li₁₋ₓCoO₂. Charging deeply beyond about x = 0.5 makes the structure unstable through changes such as in the stacking of the layers, and lattice oxygen can be released or react with the electrolyte, causing degradation and heat generation. Charging is therefore stopped at about 4.2 V to keep x near 0.5, giving 274 × 0.5 ≈ 137, about 140 mAh/g. Surface modification and elemental substitution are used to raise the cutoff voltage and increase capacity. The claim that Co³⁺ is not oxidized contradicts the charging reaction itself. Capacity is set by the amount of Li that can move in and out of the electrode, not by the Li⁺ in the electrolyte.
